title: JSON Web Encryption (JWE)
summary: JSON Web Encryption (JWE) represents encrypted content using JSON-based data structures. The cryptographic algorithms and identifiers it uses are described in the separate JSON Web Algorithms specification and IANA registries.

eli5.summary: A JWE is a locked box for data. Only someone with the right key can open it and read what is inside.

questions: what is the enc header parameter in jwe
subtitle: How to put encrypted data into a JSON-friendly package that can be compact or can serve many recipients.

tldr.problem: Applications that already use JSON need a standard way to carry encrypted content with its integrity protection, in forms that fit in places like HTTP headers or that can reach several recipients.
tldr.mechanism: A JWE holds a header, an encrypted content key, an initialization vector, the ciphertext and an authentication tag, each base64url encoded. It comes in a compact dot-separated string or as a JSON object.
tldr.outcome: Content is encrypted and integrity protected with an AEAD algorithm, and the choice of algorithms is left to the separate JWA specification and IANA registries.

today: RFC 7516 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The algorithms and key formats it relies on are defined in RFC 7518 and RFC 7517.

sections.title: What a JWE Is
sections.content:
JSON Web Encryption (JWE) represents encrypted content using JSON-based data structures. Its mechanisms encrypt and provide integrity protection for an arbitrary sequence of octets.

Two serializations are defined. The JWE Compact Serialization is a compact, URL-safe string meant for space-constrained places such as HTTP Authorization headers and URI query parameters. The JWE JSON Serialization is a JSON object that lets the same content be encrypted to multiple parties. Both share the same cryptographic underpinnings.

The algorithms themselves are not in this RFC. They are described in the JSON Web Algorithms specification (RFC 7518) and its IANA registries, and the related signature and MAC capabilities are in JSON Web Signature (RFC 7515). The names are short on purpose, because a core goal is compact output.
sections.eli5: A JWE is a way to pack a secret message so it can travel through places that only like plain text. There is a short version for tight spaces and a longer one that can be opened by several people.

sections.title: The Parts of a JWE
sections.content:
A JWE is built from six logical values: the JOSE Header, the JWE Encrypted Key, the JWE Initialization Vector, the JWE AAD, the JWE Ciphertext and the JWE Authentication Tag. Binary values are base64url encoded because JSON has no direct way to carry arbitrary octets.

Content is protected with authenticated encryption, an AEAD algorithm. It takes the plaintext and optional Additional Authenticated Data (AAD, integrity protected but not encrypted) and produces the ciphertext and an authentication tag. The symmetric key used for this is the Content Encryption Key (CEK).

The JOSE Header is the union of up to three JSON objects: the JWE Protected Header (integrity protected, applies to all recipients), the JWE Shared Unprotected Header and the JWE Per-Recipient Unprotected Header. The two unprotected ones exist only in the JSON serialization and are not integrity protected.

The JWE AAD can only be used with the JWE JSON Serialization. The RFC notes that the same effect is possible elsewhere by placing the value in an integrity-protected header parameter, at the cost of it being double base64url encoded.
sections.eli5: Think of a box with a sealed lid note (the protected header), a locked key envelope, a random starter value, the scrambled message and a stamp that proves nothing was changed. Each piece has its own job.

sections.title: The JOSE Header and Key Management
sections.content:
The header describes how the plaintext was encrypted. Two parameters are central. alg names the algorithm used to encrypt or determine the CEK. enc names the content encryption algorithm, which MUST be an AEAD algorithm with a specified key length. The enc parameter MUST be present and understood. If either value is not a supported algorithm, the content is not usable.

The optional zip parameter names a compression algorithm applied before encryption. The value defined here is DEF, meaning DEFLATE (RFC 1951). When used it MUST be integrity protected, so it appears only in the JWE Protected Header.

Other parameters (jku, jwk, kid, x5u, x5c, x5t, x5t#S256, typ, cty, crit) share their meaning with the JWS specification. The difference is that any key they point to is the public key to which the JWE was encrypted. Header parameter names MUST be unique.

The alg value implies one of five Key Management Modes: Key Encryption, Key Wrapping, Direct Key Agreement, Key Agreement with Key Wrapping, and Direct Encryption. They differ in how the CEK is produced and whether an encrypted copy of it travels in the JWE Encrypted Key.
sections.eli5: The header is a note that says which lock was used on the message and how the key to that lock is delivered. There are five ways to hand over the key.

sections.title: Compact and JSON Serializations
sections.content:
The Compact Serialization is five base64url values joined by periods: the protected header, the encrypted key, the initialization vector, the ciphertext and the authentication tag. It supports only one recipient and has no syntax for the shared or per-recipient unprotected headers or for AAD.

The JWE JSON Serialization is a JSON object with up to eight members: protected, unprotected, header, encrypted_key, iv, ciphertext, tag and aad. In its general syntax, a recipients array holds one element per recipient, each with its own header and encrypted_key. The IV, ciphertext and tag are shared, which can save significant space for large messages.

Because the content is encrypted once, every header parameter that affects the plaintext treatment, mainly enc, MUST be the same for all recipients. The flattened syntax removes the recipients array for the single-recipient case and puts header and encrypted_key at the top level. A JSON-serialized JWE is neither compact nor URL safe.
sections.eli5: The short version is one long string with five chunks separated by dots, for one reader. The long version is a labeled form that can hold a separate key envelope for each reader while sharing one scrambled message.

sections.title: Encrypting and Decrypting
sections.content:
To encrypt, the sender picks the key management mode, makes or agrees on a CEK, encrypts the CEK to the recipient if the mode requires it (otherwise the encrypted key is the empty octet sequence), and generates a random initialization vector if the algorithm needs one. It then optionally compresses the plaintext, builds the headers and sets the AAD to the ASCII of the encoded protected header. If a JWE AAD is present, the AAD becomes the encoded protected header, a period and the base64url of the JWE AAD. Finally it encrypts, producing the ciphertext and tag.

Decryption reverses this. The recipient parses the parts, base64url decodes them, checks that the protected header is valid JSON without duplicate parameter names, and verifies it understands every required field, including those listed in crit. It determines the CEK, then decrypts and validates the tag, rejecting the input without emitting any decrypted output if the tag is wrong.

With several recipients, the application decides whether all or only one must succeed, but at least one MUST succeed or the JWE MUST be considered invalid. Even a JWE that decrypts should be treated as invalid if the application does not accept the algorithms used.
sections.eli5: To send, you lock the message with a fresh key, then lock that key for the reader. To read, the reader unlocks the key, then the message, and refuses to show anything if the seal looks broken.

sections.title: Telling JWS and JWE Apart
sections.content:
JWS and JWE objects can be distinguished in several ways, and all agree for legal input. In the compact forms, a JWS has three segments separated by two periods and a JWE has five segments separated by four periods. In the JSON forms, a JWS has a payload member and a JWE has a ciphertext member.

The header also gives it away. An alg value for a signature, a MAC or none means a JWS, while a key encryption, key wrapping, key agreement or direct encryption algorithm means a JWE. If an enc member exists, it is a JWE.
sections.eli5: Count the dots. Three chunks is a signed note, five chunks is a locked box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations from the JWS specification also apply, along with those of XML Encryption 1.1 other than the XML-specific ones. Random values are needed for CEKs and initialization vectors as well as for signing. Implementations must protect the key encryption key and the CEK, since compromise of either may expose the encrypted content.

Algorithms of matching strengths should be used together. If the key encryption and content encryption algorithms differ, the effective security is determined by the weaker of the two.

The RFC warns about adaptive chosen-ciphertext attacks. An attacker might change alg from RSA-OAEP to RSA1_5 to provoke a formatting error that leaks the CEK. Defenses are to report all formatting errors in the CEK, AAD or ciphertext as a single error, and to restrict each key to a limited set of algorithms, usually one. To resist timing attacks, the recipient MUST NOT distinguish between format, padding and length errors of encrypted keys, and it is strongly recommended to substitute a random CEK on a bad key and continue.
sections.eli5: Guard both keys, match the strength of your locks, and never tell an attacker exactly how a failed attempt went wrong, because even small hints help them.
